blocks.content: A thread is the smallest unit of execution that a CPU scheduler can hand out. It is a lightweight sibling of a process: fast to create, fast to switch between, and cheap to run, because it borrows almost everything it needs from the process it lives inside.

This chapter defines what a thread actually is, explains why threads exist at all, shows exactly what a thread shares with its siblings and what it keeps to itself, walks through a real world example, and covers the sharp edges you need to know for an interview.
1. The Smallest Unit of Execution

When people talk about a program "running," they usually picture a process: a running instance of a program with its own private memory. But inside that process, the actual work of executing instructions one after another is done by something smaller called a thread. A process can hold just one thread, or it can hold many, and every process has at least one.

blocks.title: The core idea
blocks.content: A process is the container. A thread is the thing that actually runs inside that container. The operating system scheduler does not schedule processes directly, it schedules threads.
2. Definition: What a Thread Actually Is
blocks.text: 2. Definition: What a Thread Actually Is

blocks.content: A thread is a single sequential flow of execution within a process. It has its own program counter, which tracks the next instruction it is about to run, its own set of register values, and its own stack for local variables and function calls. What it does not have is its own private copy of memory. Instead, a thread shares the process's memory space, its code, and its open files with every other thread that lives inside that same process.
A thread is an independent path of execution inside a process, with its own program counter, registers, and stack, running in the same memory space as every other thread that belongs to that process.
One process, many threads

The crucial insight is that a single process can contain multiple threads, all running concurrently, each one handling a different part of the same program's work. A word processor might have one thread checking your spelling while another autosaves the document and a third redraws the screen, and all three are living inside the exact same process at the exact same time.

blocks.title: Every process starts with one
blocks.content: Even the simplest program has a thread the moment it starts running. That first thread is often called the main thread, and it can go on to create more threads if the program needs them.
3. Why Threads Exist

Creating a new process and switching the processor from one process to another is expensive. Each process needs its own separate memory space, its own page tables, and its own set of open resources, and setting all of that up takes real time and real memory. If a program simply wanted to do two things concurrently, spinning up a whole second process for the other task would be wasteful.

Threads solve this by letting a single program achieve concurrency, doing multiple things at once, without paying the full cost of a separate process for every concurrent activity. Because threads inside the same process already share memory, code, and open files, creating one is little more than allocating a small stack and a set of registers. Switching the processor from one thread to another thread in the same process is also far cheaper than switching between two different processes, since there is no need to swap out the entire memory mapping.

Threads make it natural to split a problem into concurrent pieces that all cooperate on the same data.

blocks.content: 4. What a Thread Shares Versus What It Keeps Private
blocks.text: 4. What a Thread Shares Versus What It Keeps Private

blocks.content: This is the single most important fact about threads, and it is worth stating plainly with a table. Everything about the surrounding process is shared. Everything about the act of executing right now is private.

blocks.title: Why this split makes sense
blocks.content: Two threads doing different work still need to agree on where they are in the program and what local variables they are working with right now, so those stay private. But they are both part of the same running program, so the code they run and the data they operate on stay shared.
5. A Real World Example: Inside a Web Browser
blocks.text: 5. A Real World Example: Inside a Web Browser

blocks.content: A web browser is one of the easiest places to see threads in action. While you are looking at a page, one thread is rendering the layout onto your screen, another thread is downloading images in the background so the page keeps loading, and a third thread is listening for your clicks and keystrokes so the page stays responsive. All three of these threads belong to the very same browser process.

Because they are threads and not separate processes, all three share the same process memory, including things like the currently loaded page data, the parsed layout tree, and the browser's cache. Yet each thread has its own independent execution path, its own stack, and its own program counter, so the rendering thread can be in the middle of drawing a box while the network thread is somewhere completely different, waiting on a socket.

6. The Power and Danger of Shared Memory
blocks.text: 6. The Power and Danger of Shared Memory

blocks.content: Sharing memory is what makes threads fast to communicate with each other. If one thread produces a result, another thread can read it directly, with no copying and no message passing required, because they are already looking at the same memory. This is one of the biggest reasons threads are chosen over separate processes for tightly cooperating work.

That same direct access is also what makes threads dangerous. Because every thread in a process can read and write the same shared memory, a bug in one thread, such as writing to the wrong variable or updating shared data at the wrong moment, can corrupt data that another thread is relying on. This kind of corruption simply cannot happen between two separate processes, because processes have fully isolated memory and one cannot reach into the other's space by accident.

blocks.title: The tradeoff in one line
blocks.content: Threads trade the safety of isolation for the speed of shared memory. That tradeoff is exactly why topics like race conditions, locks, and synchronization exist as their own chapters.
7. Common Misconceptions

A very common misconception is assuming that threads always run truly simultaneously. That is only true on a multi core processor, where different cores can genuinely execute different threads at the exact same instant. On a single core processor, only one thread can ever be running at any given moment. The operating system rapidly switches the processor between threads, giving each one a short slice of time, and the switching happens so fast that the threads only appear to be running simultaneously.

["Threads are not automatically faster just because there are more of them, especially on a single core machine.","Threads sharing memory does not mean they always see perfectly consistent data without careful coordination.","A thread crashing can bring down the entire process, since it shares that process's memory with every other thread."]
items: Threads are not automatically faster just because there are more of them, especially on a single core machine.
Threads sharing memory does not mean they always see perfectly consistent data without careful coordination.
A thread crashing can bring down the entire process, since it shares that process's memory with every other thread.

blocks.content: 8. The Interview Angle

A very common first follow up question after defining a thread is "how is that different from a process." That comparison deserves its own full treatment, and it is covered in the sibling Process vs Thread topic in this course. For now, the short version is that a process is an isolated, independent unit with its own memory, while a thread is a lightweight unit of execution that shares memory with the other threads in its process. Keep that forward pointer in mind rather than trying to answer the full comparison here.

blocks.title: What to remember for interviews
blocks.content: A thread has its own program counter, registers, and stack. It shares code, data, heap, and open files with every other thread in the same process. That single fact answers most follow up questions about threads.
